title: Cough and Chest Tightness – Maria Gomez
chief_complaint: Persistent cough and chest tightness for three weeks

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Good morning, Maria. What brings you in today?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: Hi, Dr. Patel. I've had this cough for about three weeks now, and lately it’s been tight in my chest, especially at night.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Got it. Did it start after anything in particular?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: Actually, yeah. I moved into a new apartment right after it was repainted, and we adopted a cat the same week. Also, the wildfire smoke last month really irritated my throat.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: What tends to make it worse or better?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: Running, dusting, or being around the litter box definitely make it worse. Perfumes too. The humidifier and honey-lemon tea help a little.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Is it mostly dry or are you bringing anything up?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: Mostly dry, maybe a little clear phlegm in the mornings.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Any fevers, shortness of breath, or wheezing?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: Wheezing, yes, especially when I lie down. No fever. Sometimes I feel a tightness but not real pain.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Have symptoms improved, worsened, or stayed the same?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: They’ve gotten worse in the last ten days. I’m waking up coughing several nights a week.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Any recent travel or exposures?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: I went to Denver two weeks ago, just for the weekend. No sick contacts. At home, the bathroom ceiling has some mold — I told my landlord.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Any medications, allergies, or supplements?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: I take sertraline 50 mg daily and a birth control pill. I’m allergic to amoxicillin — gives me a rash.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Have you tried anything for the cough?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: Cetirizine, fluticasone nasal spray, tea, humidifier. They help a little, but not enough.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Any side effects or concerns about medications?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: Yeah, I had prednisone once for a rash — made me jittery and my heart raced, so I stopped early. I’m nervous about steroids.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Totally fair. Any asthma or allergy history?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: I had eczema as a kid but no asthma diagnosis. Dust and pollen make me sneeze sometimes.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Tell me about your living situation and support system.

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: I live with a roommate, my boyfriend helps a lot. No smokers in the house. I work as a kindergarten teacher, so I talk all day — the coughing gets in the way, and I’m tired from poor sleep.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: That sounds exhausting. How’s this affecting your exercise or mood?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: I’ve had to pause my 5K training. It’s frustrating — I just want to breathe normally again.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Have you ever declined or stopped any treatments for this kind of issue?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: My old doctor suggested an inhaled steroid a few years ago, but I didn’t start it because of how prednisone made me feel.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Understood. Let’s check your vitals and lungs.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Vitals are stable — BP 116/72, HR 88, RR 18, Temp 98.2°F, SpO₂ 98%. Mild end-expiratory wheezes at both bases, no crackles.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: This could be cough-variant or allergic asthma. We’ll run a few tests to confirm.

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: Okay.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: I’ll order spirometry, a CBC with eosinophils, total IgE, and allergy testing. Maybe full pulmonary function tests later.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: For now, let’s try a low-dose ICS–formoterol inhaler, used as needed and before exercise. It’s localized — minimal systemic effects.

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: That sounds fine. I just don’t want to feel jittery or gain weight.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Perfectly reasonable. We can start low and monitor.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: I’ll also send a letter to your landlord about mold remediation and recommend a HEPA air purifier.

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: Thank you — that’d help.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Any issues with medication cost or insurance?

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: Sometimes prior authorizations take weeks. If there’s a coupon, that’d be great.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: I’ll attach one and handle the paperwork.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: Let’s follow up in two weeks to review symptoms and test results. If you have severe shortness of breath, blue lips, or can’t speak full sentences, go to urgent care or the ER.

content.speaker: Maria
content.text: Got it, thanks so much.

content.speaker: Dr. Patel
content.text: You’re welcome — feel better, Maria.
